title: Features, point-in-time correctness and data contracts
summary: A feature row has an entity, a time it describes and a time it became usable: join on the second, decide missing values by cause, keep one transformation for training and serving, and verify platform feature capabilities after the mechanism.
outcomes: Define a feature by its entity key, window, transformation and inputs, and write a feature contract that code can check.
Build a point-in-time training set on availability time and diagnose event-time joins, latest-value lookups and overwrite backfills as future-data leakage.
Apply one missingness and freshness policy in training and serving, and detect training/serving skew with consistency checks on edge-case inputs.
Choose batch, online or on-demand feature delivery from the decision, and map each mechanism onto documented Databricks Feature Store capabilities with their caveats.
startingAssumptions: The machine-learning fundamentals module has defined a prediction time, a label horizon and leakage from fields written after the fact.
You can read SQL joins and GROUP BY aggregations and a short pandas program.
editorialRationale: Feature teaching fails when it starts from a product: learners then see a feature store as the solution to a problem they cannot state. The module first makes a feature row concrete (entity, window, value), adds the second time that decides usability, and only then builds the point-in-time join and its two classic leaks. Keys, missingness, contracts, skew and late data follow as separate failure modes, each tied to one executed lab result, before reuse and delivery choices. Databricks Feature Store capabilities come last, mapped onto the mechanism with their documented conditions, including the online lookback gap and preview status, and the module closes on how to prove point-in-time correctness honestly.

concepts.definition: A named value computed by a transformation from raw data for one entity as of one time, used as a model input.
concepts.example: temp_mean_2h = 70.0 for PR-02 over the window ending 10:00.

concepts.definition: The first moment a feature value could be read by a consumer, after ingestion and computation, as distinct from the time it describes.
concepts.example: PR-02's 10:00 window is available at 10:30, when the scheduled run publishes it.

concepts.definition: A join that gives each labelled row the newest feature value of the same entity that was available at or before its prediction time.
concepts.example: PR-02 at 10:15 receives the 08:00 window, published at 08:30.

concepts.definition: Reading each entity's newest feature value regardless of time; correct at request time, a leak when building historical rows.
concepts.example: A 09:00 training row reading PR-01's 12:00 window published at 12:30.

concepts.definition: The column or columns naming the thing a feature describes, which must match exactly across features, labels and requests.
concepts.example: machine_id PR-02, never pr-02, in every table and request.

concepts.definition: A written rule per cause of an absent feature value stating what training and serving each do with it.
concepts.example: No row yet is none_available and excluded; an empty vibration column stays null.

concepts.definition: The producer's checkable promise about a feature table's keys, time meanings, units, null semantics, bounds and publication cadence.
concepts.example: vib_count_2h between 0 and reading_count_2h; source_max_ingested_at never after available_at.

concepts.definition: A difference between the feature values a model saw in training and those it receives in serving for the same entity and moment.
concepts.example: Training keeps PR-03's vibration null; a serving port sends 0.0.

concepts.definition: An appended row for the same entity and window with a later availability time, published when late inputs change the value.

concepts.definition: The age of a feature value when used, the prediction time minus the time the value describes, judged against a consumer's limit.

concepts.definition: Precomputing features for scheduled scoring versus looking them up with low latency when a request arrives.

questions.prompt: The feature row (PR-02, feature_time 10:00, temp_mean_2h 70.0) was computed from readings at 08:30, 09:10 and 10:00. Which statement about it is accurate?

options.text: It is PR-02's temperature at exactly 10:00.
options.rationale: It is a mean over three readings; the 10:00 reading alone was 72.

options.text: It summarizes PR-02's readings in the window (08:00, 10:00]; the machine and the window end identify the row.
options.rationale: The row describes one entity over one window; its identity is the key, not the value 70.0.

options.text: Any model could read it from 10:00, when the window ended.
options.rationale: The window end says what the row describes, not when it became readable; the next beat shows the row appears later than 10:00.

options.text: It applies to every press that reported in that window.
options.rationale: The entity key limits the value to PR-02; PR-03's window has its own row with a different mean.

questions.prompt: To decide whether a feature row may be used by a labelled training row, which pair of times must be compared?

options.text: The feature row's feature_time against the training row's prediction_time.
options.rationale: The window end says what the row describes, not when it existed; it admits the 10:00 window at 10:15.

options.text: The newest reading's observed_at against the training row's label_time.
options.rationale: The label time is when the outcome became known, hours after the prediction; it admits almost everything.

options.text: The feature row's available_at against the training row's prediction_time.
options.rationale: Availability is the first moment a model could read the row; the prediction time is when the model would have asked.

options.text: The feature row's feature_time against the training row's label_time.
options.rationale: Neither time is the decision moment; this comparison admits rows published after the prediction.

questions.prompt: PR-03 was commissioned at 09:00; its only window ends at 10:00 and is published at 10:30. What does a point-in-time join return for a PR-03 prediction at 10:20?

options.text: No feature row: the label row is kept with null features and the status none_available.
options.rationale: Nothing of PR-03's was published by 10:20, and an honest training row records exactly that.

options.text: The 10:00 window, 61.0 °C, because that window ended before 10:20.
options.rationale: That is the event-time join; the row was published at 10:30, ten minutes after the prediction.

options.text: PR-02's 08:00 window, the newest row published by 10:20.
options.rationale: The join matches machine_id first; another press's row describes a different entity.

options.text: An error, because merge_asof cannot return an unmatched row.
options.rationale: A backward as-of join leaves the right-hand columns null when no row qualifies; it does not raise.

questions.prompt: A notebook builds last quarter's training set by joining each labelled row to a current_features view holding one row per machine. Offline recall jumps. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The view is fresher, so the model genuinely learned a stronger signal.
options.rationale: Fresher than the decision is impossible for a live model; the gain cannot be reproduced in serving.

options.text: The view removed duplicate rows, which reduced noise.
options.rationale: One row per machine discards history rather than noise; the timing drives the gain.

options.text: Recall rose because the label horizon changed.
options.rationale: Nothing in the change touched the labels; only the feature lookup changed.

options.text: Historical rows received values published after their prediction times, so the jump measures future-data leakage.
options.rationale: A current view is the point-in-time answer only at serving time; for past rows it carries later information.

questions.prompt: The feature table holds two rows for (PR-01, feature_time 10:00, available_at 10:30): 77.0 and 99.0. The join keeps the last matching row. What should the pipeline do?

options.text: Average the two rows to 88.0 and continue.
options.rationale: An average invents a value that no run produced and hides a producer defect.

options.text: Refuse the table with an error naming the key, because the value used would depend on storage order.
options.rationale: The lab shows 99.0 on one file order and 77.0 on the reverse; only the producer can say which is true.

options.text: Keep the larger value, because failures correlate with heat.
options.rationale: Choosing by the target's direction is a biased rule that no serving path would reproduce.

options.text: Trust the declared PRIMARY KEY to have prevented it.
options.rationale: Primary key constraints on Databricks are informational and not enforced, so the duplicate can exist.

questions.prompt: PR-03's only window has two readings and no vibration value. Which feature row follows the module's missingness policy?

options.text: reading_count_2h 2, vib_count_2h 2, vib_max_2h 0.0.
options.rationale: That is zero-filling: it reports two vibration measurements of zero that never happened.

options.text: No row at all, because a feature is missing.
options.rationale: Temperature was measured twice; dropping the row discards real data and turns the window into none_available.

options.text: reading_count_2h 2, vib_count_2h 0, vib_max_2h null, low_coverage true.
options.rationale: The counts say what arrived, the null says nothing was measured and the flag records the thin window.

options.text: vib_max_2h set to the mean vibration of all presses over the whole day.
options.rationale: A whole-day mean uses readings from after this window and from other entities: it leaks and fabricates.

questions.prompt: A consistency check between the training transformation and a serving port passes on the 08:30 run and fails on the 10:30 run. What is the best reading?

options.text: The 10:30 run is corrupt, because the port agreed earlier.
options.rationale: The training transformation produced the contract's values at 10:30; the disagreement sits in the port.

options.text: Floating-point noise; loosen the tolerance until both runs pass.
options.rationale: A count of 3 against 2 and null against 0.0 are not rounding differences.

options.text: Only the 08:30 run matters, because training uses older data.
options.rationale: Serving computes every window, including those with boundary readings and missing values.

options.text: The port has drifted; the 08:30 inputs lacked the boundary reading and missing values that expose it.
options.rationale: Agreement is shown only for inputs that were compared; the 10:30 inputs contain the edge cases.

questions.prompt: PR-01's 09:50 reading is ingested at 11:05, and the 11:30 run publishes version 2 of the 10:00 window (78.0). Which PR-01 training rows should change: 11:00, 11:45, 12:45?

options.text: Only 11:45: it follows version 2's publication and the 10:00 window is still its newest.
options.rationale: At 11:00 the reading had not arrived, and at 12:45 the 12:00 window is newer.

options.text: 11:00 and 11:45, because both use the 10:00 window.
options.rationale: At 11:00 version 2 did not exist; changing that row imports a reading from 11:05.

options.text: All three, because the corrected value is more accurate.
options.rationale: Accuracy after the fact is not what a live model had, and 12:45 uses a different window.

options.text: None, because published rows are never rewritten.
options.rationale: Rows are never rewritten, but a new version is appended and later predictions use it.

questions.prompt: A Databricks time series feature table stores the window end (10:00) as its timestamp key; values are published 30 minutes after each window ends. A point-in-time lookup runs for a training row at 10:15. What does it return?

options.text: The 08:00 window, because the lookup knows the 30-minute publication delay.
options.rationale: The lookup sees only the timestamp key; the delay is recorded nowhere in the table.

options.text: Null, because a lookback window is always applied.
options.rationale: lookback_window defaults to None, and when set it removes old values, not future ones.

options.text: The 10:00 window's values, which no live model could read until 10:30: a leak unless the key holds publication time.
options.rationale: The lookup returns the latest value prior to 10:15 by the timestamp key, and the key says 10:00.

options.text: An error, because timestamp keys must be dates.
options.rationale: A timestamp key may be TimestampType or DateType.

questions.prompt: Training used FeatureLookup(..., lookback_window=timedelta(hours=3)). In production, PR-03's newest online value is five hours old when a request arrives. According to the point-in-time documentation, what does online inference use?

options.text: Null, matching training, because the lookback window travels with the model.
options.rationale: That consistency is exactly what the documentation says does not happen during online inference.

options.text: The latest value, five hours old: the lookback window is not applied online, so the caller must enforce the age rule.
options.rationale: The documentation states the lookback window applies during training and batch inference only.

options.text: An error that forces the application to retry.
options.rationale: Nothing in the lookup treats an old value as an error.

options.text: A value recomputed from raw readings at request time.
options.rationale: Only on-demand features are computed at request time; published features are looked up.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline adds oil_particles_ppm from lab samples: a sample is drawn at the press, analysed in a lab and entered hours later. Write five contract lines for this feature and say which are checked when rows are written and which when training rows are read.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Key: machine_id, sampled_at and result_entered_at are unique together, refused as duplicates at write. Time meanings: sampled_at is what the value describes and result_entered_at is when it became usable; the join uses result_entered_at and the read-side guard refuses later rows. Units and bounds: ppm between 0 and the lab's stated maximum, enforced at write, for example by a CHECK constraint. Null meaning: an unanalysed sample has no row, never 0 ppm, checked at write. Freshness belongs to each consumer: every model states its maximum sample age and applies it at read.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Each line is testable and sits where the data to test it exists; putting one model's maximum age into the producer contract would impose it on every consumer. Adding the lab method version to the key is an acceptable extension.

selfQuestions.prompt: The handover model predicts at 10:00 and 12:00 with a 90-minute limit, and no training row is usable. A colleague proposes joining on window end so the 10:00 prediction gets the 10:00 window. Explain why you refuse and propose two fixes.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Joining on window end gives the 10:00 prediction a row published at 10:30, so training would use information a live model at 10:00 cannot have; offline results would be optimistic and irreproducible. Instead, move the decision after a publication, for example to 10:35 when the 10:00 window is 35 minutes old, or shift the window grid so windows end at 09:30 and are published by 10:00, giving a 30-minute age at the handover. Computing the value on request from raw readings is a third option if those readings reach serving.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The refusal names the leak and its consequence, and each fix changes when data exists or when the decision happens instead of pretending data existed earlier. Relaxing the limit is acceptable only as the model owner's explicit decision.

selfQuestions.prompt: Cinderline wants a daily 06:00 maintenance priority list and an alert when an operator scans a die into a press. For each, choose batch scoring, online lookup or on-demand computation for its features, and say what you would monitor.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: The 06:00 list is batch: join features as of 06:00, store predictions with the model version and the newest available_at used, and monitor that the run finished and that feature ages stayed within the limit. The die-scan alert needs online lookup for the sensor windows plus on-demand computation for the die identity and scan time known only in the request; monitor sync lag and the age of served rows, and log request inputs so training can recompute the on-demand value the same way.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The choice follows decision timing and request-time inputs, and each path names its own silent failure. Serving the list from an online store also works but adds a copy and a sync with no benefit.

selfQuestions.prompt: A colleague calls a feature pipeline point-in-time correct because validation AUC is stable across three reruns. What evidence would you ask for instead, and what would that evidence still not prove?
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: Stable AUC shows repeatability, not correctness; a leaky join repeats perfectly. I would ask for a guard asserting every joined row was published by its prediction time with lineage checked, tests showing that an event-time join, a latest-value lookup, a duplicate key and a backfill each fail for their named reason, and a late-data rerun listing the changed rows. Even then it would not prove the features predict failure, behave the same at scale, or match the platform in the target workspace.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The answer separates repeatability from correctness and asks for failing tests, the only proof that a guard bites. Adding a forward-period evaluation to the request is a good extension.

beats.title: A feature is a value computed for an entity as of a time
beats.outcome: Name the entity key, the window, the transformation and the inputs behind a feature value before using it.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-features-feature-concept|feature]] is not a column you find; it is a value a transformation computes for one entity over one period. Cinderline's job turns PR-02's three readings between 08:00 and 10:00 into one row: machine_id PR-02, feature_time 10:00, temp_mean_2h 70.0, vib_count_2h 2. Notice in the first state that the 10:00:00 reading belongs to the window it closes, and in the third that the machine and the window end identify the row, not the value.
beats.hint: Which two fields name the row, and which field is only a value?

handbook.markdown:
A feature definition has four parts: the entity it describes (`machine_id`), the period it covers (a two-hour window closed on the right), the transformation (mean temperature, maximum vibration, two counts) and the inputs it may read (readings ingested before the job runs). Write all four down before arguing about model quality; most feature defects are a wrong part, not a wrong algorithm.

```python
known = observations[observations["ingested_at"] <= run_at].copy()  # ingested by the run
known["feature_time"] = known["observed_at"].dt.ceil("2h")  # (start, end]
known = known[known["feature_time"] <= run_at]  # windows closed by the run
rows = known.groupby(["machine_id", "feature_time"]).agg(
    temp_mean_2h=("temp_c", "mean"),
    vib_max_2h=("vibration_mm_s", "max"),
    reading_count_2h=("temp_c", "size"),
    vib_count_2h=("vibration_mm_s", "count"))
```

In SQL the same row is a `GROUP BY machine_id, window_end` with `AVG`, `MAX`, `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(vibration_mm_s)`. `COUNT(column)` skips NULLs as pandas `count` does, and `COUNT(*)` counts rows like `size`; the pair lets PR-02's row say three readings arrived but only two carried a vibration value.

Boundaries are part of the definition. `ceil` keeps a 10:00:00 reading in the window ending 10:00; `floor` plus two hours pushes it into the next window. Either convention can be chosen, but training and serving must share one and the contract must name it.

What to inspect first: the grain (one row per entity per window?), the boundary rule, how missing inputs are counted, and whether the row carries enough keys to be joined later. What the value cannot tell you is when the row became usable, which is the next beat's subject. The lab's fixtures reproduce every number here.

beats.recap: Entity, window, transformation and inputs define a feature; the value alone defines nothing.

beats.title: Every feature row carries the time it describes and the time it became usable
beats.outcome: Place readings, window ends, publication times, prediction times and label times on one timeline and say which rows a prediction may use.
beats.explanation: The machine-learning fundamentals module separated when a reading happened from when it arrived. A computed feature adds a second delay: Cinderline's job publishes each window 30 minutes after it closes. So every row needs [[dbxfe-features-availability-concept|availability time]], available_at, beside feature_time. Labels carry their own times too: a prediction time and a later time when the outcome is known. Notice in the second state that at 10:15 the 10:00 window does not exist yet, and in the third that a late reading adds a version.

samajh.text: Socho raat 10 baje ek match khatam hua. Uski khabar subah 6 baje ke akhbaar mein chhapti hai. Khabar 10 baje ki hai, par padhne ke liye subah se pehle kahin available nahi thi. Agar koi poochhe ki raat 11 baje aapko kya pata tha, toh subah ka akhbaar us jawab mein nahi aa sakta, chahe usme kal raat ki hi baat likhi ho.
samajh.mapping: The match ending at 10 pm is feature_time, the morning edition is available_at and the 11 pm question is the prediction time.
samajh.boundary: A newspaper is printed once; a feature row can be republished as a new version when late inputs arrive, each version with its own availability time.

handbook.markdown:
Four clocks meet in a training row. `observed_at` is when a sensor measured; `ingested_at` is when the reading landed; `available_at` is when the feature job published a row that used it; `prediction_time` is when the model would have been asked. A row may feed a prediction only if `available_at <= prediction_time`. For Cinderline the delays stack: readings land about two minutes after measurement, the 10:00 window is computed at the 10:30 run, and a flaky gateway delivered PR-01's 09:50 reading at 11:05.

Labels have their own times. PR-01 fails at 14:10, so its predictions at 11:00, 11:45 and 12:45 are positives, known at 14:10. A negative is known only when its four-hour horizon has passed: PR-03's 13:30 prediction is known at 17:30. A training set cut at 17:00 must leave that row out rather than read 'no failure yet' as 'no failure'. Positives become known earlier than negatives, so an early cutoff over-represents failures.

| time | event |
|---|---|
| 10:00 | window (08:00, 10:00] closes |
| 10:15 | PR-02 prediction: newest usable row is the 08:00 window |
| 10:30 | 10:00 window published |
| 11:05 | late PR-01 reading ingested |
| 11:30 | PR-01 10:00 window, version 2 |

What to inspect: whether the feature table stores `available_at` at all. If it stores only the window end, what was knowable cannot be reconstructed and every later check is guesswork. Saying it to a maintenance lead: 'the 10:00 summary exists from 10:30; a 10:15 decision could not have seen it, so training must not either.'

beats.recap: Join on when a row became usable, and train only on labels already known.

beats.title: The training join asks what was published by the prediction time
beats.outcome: Build a point-in-time join with merge_asof or an explicit filter and predict its output for delayed and missing rows.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-features-pit-concept|point-in-time join]] gives each labelled row the newest feature row of the same entity whose availability is at or before the prediction time. Notice the second state: joined on the window end, PR-02 at 10:15 and PR-03 at 10:20 receive the 10:00 windows, published at 10:30. The third state joins on availability: PR-02 gets the 08:00 window, 135 minutes old, and PR-03 gets nothing, which is the honest answer.

samajh.text: Bank passbook yaad karo. Har line ki ek date hoti hai jab woh print hui. Koi poochhe ki 5 tareekh ko aapka balance kya tha, toh aap 5 tareekh tak print hui aakhri line padhoge. Baad mein print hui line, chahe woh 3 tareekh ke kisi cheque ki ho, 5 tareekh ke jawab mein nahi aati, kyunki us din woh passbook mein thi hi nahi.
samajh.mapping: Passbook lines are published feature rows, the print date is available_at and the date asked about is the prediction time.
samajh.boundary: A passbook covers one account; a feature join also matches the entity key and prefers the newest window before the newest version.

handbook.markdown:
In pandas the join is one call, provided both frames are sorted by their time keys and the entity is passed as `by`:

```python
train = pd.merge_asof(
    labels.sort_values("prediction_time"),
    features.sort_values("available_at"),
    left_on="prediction_time", right_on="available_at",
    by="machine_id", direction="backward", allow_exact_matches=True)
```

`direction='backward'` selects the last right-hand row whose key is less than or equal to the left key; `allow_exact_matches=True` lets a row published at 10:30 serve a 10:30 prediction. Setting it to `False` means strictly earlier, a policy to state rather than inherit.

In SQL, join on `machine_id` with `f.available_at <= l.prediction_time` and keep one row per label by `ROW_NUMBER()` ordered by `feature_time` then `available_at`, both descending.

Why the explicit order matters: `merge_asof` on `available_at` returns the most recently published row, which is the newest window only while no older window is republished later. In the lab a late reading republished PR-02's 08:00 window at 12:30, and `merge_asof` then handed the 12:45 prediction that older row, 285 minutes old. The explicit rule, newest window first and newest version second, kept the 10:00 window. Test both on data with a late republication.

What fails: joining on `feature_time`, forgetting `by`, unsorted inputs (`merge_asof` raises) and key columns with different time zones or resolutions. What to inspect: assert `available_at <= prediction_time` for every joined row, count unmatched rows per entity, and list each chosen row's age. An empty match is data: PR-03 was commissioned at 09:00 and had nothing published until 10:30.

beats.recap: Each training row takes the newest row published by its own prediction time, or honestly none.

beats.title: The newest value is right when serving and a leak in history
beats.outcome: Explain why a latest-value lookup is correct at request time and leaks future data when it builds training rows.
beats.explanation: At serving time the model asks now, so each machine's newest published row is exactly the point-in-time answer. The same [[dbxfe-features-latest-concept|latest-value lookup]] run today over history is not. Notice in the second state that the 09:00 training row receives PR-01's 12:00 window, published at 12:30, three and a half hours after the decision. In the lab this lookup was wrong for seven of eleven training rows, while the point-in-time join and the online lookup agreed on all eleven.

handbook.markdown:
Leakage through a latest-value lookup is common because the lookup is correct somewhere. An online store holds one current row per entity, a serving request reads it, and the request time is the prediction time: nothing leaks. Reuse that lookup to assemble last month's training set and every historical row receives values published after its decision. Offline metrics improve for exactly the rows a live model will never see.

The rule is one sentence: evaluate every lookup as of the row's own prediction time. Serving is the special case where that time is now. This also gives a test that ties serving to training: call the online path at each labelled prediction time against the table as it was, and require every field to equal the training row. The lab does this at all eleven label times, before and after the late readings.

Signs of this leak in a review: a feature table without availability times, a training query with no time predicate, a join to a 'current' or 'latest' view, a feature whose importance collapses in production, and a model that looks best on the most recent history. What to inspect: take three historical training rows and check by hand the publication time of every feature value they carry.

Explaining it: 'At 09:00 the 12:00 summary did not exist. A model trained on it learned from the future; the live model will receive the 08:00 summary instead.' The fundamentals module showed the same trap with a repair code written after a failure; here the value itself is legitimate and only its timing is wrong.

beats.recap: Latest is the point-in-time answer only when the prediction time is now.

beats.title: An entity key and a time key must identify exactly one row
beats.outcome: Refuse duplicate entity-time rows and unknown entity keys before any join and name the offending key.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-features-entity-concept|entity key]] names what a feature describes; with the time keys it must identify exactly one row. Notice in the second state that two rows for PR-01's 10:00 window published at 10:30 make the join return 99.0 or 77.0 depending on storage order. The third state shows the opposite failure: a label written pr-02 matches nothing, so every feature would look missing. Both are contract errors to refuse, not values to average or impute.

handbook.markdown:
Uniqueness has to be checked, not assumed. On Databricks, primary key and foreign key constraints are informational: the documentation states they are not enforced, while Delta Lake enforces CHECK and NOT NULL constraints. A feature table can declare `PRIMARY KEY (machine_id, available_at TIMESERIES)` and still receive duplicate rows, so the pipeline must refuse them.

```python
dup = features[features.duplicated(["machine_id", "feature_time", "available_at"], keep=False)]
if not dup.empty:
    raise DuplicateEntityTimeError("duplicate entity-time feature row: ...")  # name keys and count
```

Apply the same check at three grains: readings `(machine_id, observed_at)`, feature rows `(machine_id, feature_time, available_at)` and labels `(machine_id, prediction_time)`. A duplicate reading inflates counts and shifts means, a duplicate feature row makes the join order-dependent, and a duplicate label double-weights an example.

Key matching is the other half. Entity keys must be identical across labels, features and serving requests; case, padding, leading zeros and renamed assets break the match silently, and the damage looks like missingness. Validate label and request keys against a registry of known entities, and alert when the share of `none_available` rows jumps for one entity.

What to inspect: duplicate counts per key, the set difference between label keys and feature keys, and `none_available` rates by entity. Explaining it: 'Two different numbers claimed to be PR-01's 10:00 summary; we cannot train on a coin toss, so the job stops and names the key.' Exact re-deliveries of one reading may be dropped by a tested ingestion rule, as the ingestion module's resolver does; conflicting values never can.

beats.recap: One entity, one time key, one row; anything else is refused by name.

beats.title: Missing values need a cause before they get a rule
beats.outcome: Classify each missing feature by cause and apply one written policy in training and serving.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-features-missing-concept|missingness policy]] starts from why a value is absent. Notice the first state: no row yet, a row too old for this consumer, a present row with an empty column, a thin window and an unknown key each get a different rule. The second state applies it to eleven labelled rows: eight usable, two none_available, one stale. The third shows what zero-filling would claim: PR-03's absent vibration becomes a perfectly smooth press.

samajh.text: Doctor ke paas report aayi, par ek test ka result abhi lab se nahi aaya. Woh wahan 'pending' likhega, 'normal' nahi. Aur agar report teen mahine purani hai, toh use purani maan kar naya test mangwayega. Khaali jagah ko zero ya normal likh dena ek aisa jhooth hai jo aage ke har faisle mein chala jaata hai.
samajh.mapping: A pending result is none_available, a three-month-old report is stale and writing normal in the blank is zero-filling a missing feature.
samajh.boundary: A doctor can order a new test at once; a model at serving time cannot create a missing reading and must follow the stated fallback.

handbook.markdown:
Write the policy as a table that the training code and the serving code both implement, then test both against it.

| cause | detected by | training | serving |
|---|---|---|---|
| no row yet | nothing published by the prediction time | exclude, `none_available` | no score; fallback rule |
| too old | age over the consumer's limit (180 min, inclusive) | exclude, `stale` | same limit, same fallback |
| empty column | `vib_count_2h = 0`, `vib_max_2h` null | keep null | keep null |
| thin window | `reading_count_2h < 3` | keep, `low_coverage` | same flag |
| unknown key | not in the entity registry | refuse | refuse |

Age is prediction time minus window end: PR-03 at 13:00 is exactly 180 minutes old and `ok`; at 13:30 it is 210 and `stale`. The boundary belongs to the policy and must be identical in both paths.

Imputation is a choice, not a default. If a model cannot accept nulls, fit any imputer on training rows only and apply the fitted values everywhere, as the scikit-learn pitfalls guide requires of every preprocessing step, and keep an indicator column so the model can tell filled from measured. One documented trap: `SimpleImputer(add_indicator=True)` creates indicators only for features that had missing values during fit, so a column missing only at serving time gets no indicator.

Why not zero? Zero is a measurement. Filling PR-03's absent vibration with 0.0 tells the model the press ran perfectly smooth; zero-filling a new machine's missing row makes it look cold and idle. What to inspect: counts per status per entity per day, and the same counts from serving logs; a divergence between them is skew.

beats.recap: Name the cause, then apply one rule in both paths; zero is a measurement, not a blank.

beats.title: A feature contract is checked where rows are written and where they are read
beats.outcome: Write a feature contract and place each rule at the write step or the read step that can enforce it.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-features-contract-concept|feature contract]] is the producer's promise in checkable form: entity and time keys, what each time means, units, what null means, bounds and publication cadence. Notice in the second state that the write step refuses a backfilled row claiming 10:30 while using a reading ingested at 11:05. The third state shows the read step: the join guard refuses any training row using a feature published after its prediction time. Neither check replaces the other.

handbook.markdown:
A useful contract fits on one page and every line is testable. Lab L18's `feature_contract.json` states: entities PR-01 to PR-03; key `(machine_id, feature_time, available_at)`; two-hour windows closed on the right; runs at half past each hour; three expected readings per window; `temp_mean_2h` between −40 and 150 °C; `vib_count_2h` between 0 and `reading_count_2h`; `vib_max_2h` null exactly when no vibration value arrived; `low_coverage` equal to `reading_count_2h < 3`; and a lineage rule, `source_max_ingested_at <= available_at`.

Write-side checks run before rows are published: duplicates, bounds, null meaning, grid alignment, lineage. On Databricks, Delta CHECK constraints can enforce row-level bounds at write time; uniqueness and cross-row rules need pipeline code because primary keys are informational. Read-side checks run in each consumer: label keys against the entity registry, no label describing the past (`event_at` after `prediction_time`), and the future-information guard over every joined row.

The lineage rule is the one teams skip and regret. A backfill that recomputes history from today's data and stamps nominal publication times produces rows that look punctual; only the latest ingestion time of the inputs reveals that PR-01's 10:00 row, stamped 10:30, used a reading that arrived at 11:05. Without that [[dbxfe-features-lineage-concept|lineage timestamp]] nobody can detect the leak afterwards.

Consumer policy is not producer contract: maximum feature age, training cutoff and fallback belong to each model. Version the contract; a new column, window length or boundary rule is a new version that consumers adopt deliberately. Explaining it: 'The table promises what each row means and when it existed; the job refuses anything that breaks the promise, and the model refuses anything from after its decision.'

beats.recap: Producers check what rows mean before publishing; consumers check when rows existed before training.

beats.title: Training and serving must run one transformation, not two lookalikes
beats.outcome: Detect training/serving skew with a consistency check over edge-case inputs and prefer one shared transformation.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-features-skew-concept|Training/serving skew]] appears when the serving path computes a feature differently from training. Notice the second state: a serving port that buckets readings by window start and fills absent vibration with 0.0 disagrees at 10:30 on two windows, PR-02's mean 70.0 against 69.0 and PR-03's vibration null against 0.0. The third state is the trap: at 08:30 no boundary reading or missing value had arrived, so the same broken port agreed.

samajh.text: Do darzi ek hi grahak ka naap likh rahe hain. Ek inch wale tape se naapta hai, doosra purane cm tape se, aur kamar ki jagah dono thodi alag maante hain. Aam grahakon par dono ke naap mil jaate hain, sab khush. Phir ek grahak aata hai jiski kamar theek seam par hai, aur kurta tight nikalta hai. Ek hi tape, ek hi tareeka, aur test ke liye mushkil wala grahak chahiye.
samajh.mapping: The two tailors are the training transformation and the serving port, the easy customers are the 08:30 inputs and the customer on the seam is the reading at exactly 10:00.
samajh.boundary: A tailor can remeasure the customer; a served prediction cannot be recomputed after the fact, so the check must run before release and on logged traffic.

handbook.markdown:
The scikit-learn pitfalls guide states the rule for preprocessing: a transform used in training must be applied to test and production data too, learnt from training data only. For features the stronger form is 'import, do not re-implement'. Google's Rules of Machine Learning names the failure training-serving skew and recommends sharing code between the pipelines and avoiding two programming languages, because shared code is the cheapest guarantee of consistency.

When a port is unavoidable, for example a low-latency service in another language, pin it with a check:

```python
expected = compute_features(obs, run_at, contract).set_index(["machine_id", "feature_time"])
actual = compute_features_port(obs, run_at, contract).set_index(["machine_id", "feature_time"])
# compare the union of keys and every feature column; null equals null
```

The lab's check lists each differing window and column with both values: PR-02 at 10:00 differs in `temp_mean_2h` (70.0 against 69.0), `vib_max_2h` (1.9 against 1.7), `reading_count_2h` (3 against 2) and `low_coverage`; PR-03 in `vib_max_2h` (null against 0.0) and `vib_count_2h` (0 against 2). Two drifts explain all six: a [start, end) window rule moved the 10:00:00 reading, and a fill turned 'not measured' into 'measured zero'.

A check is only as good as its inputs. Build a fixture containing every edge the contract names: a reading on a boundary, a missing value, an empty window, a late reading and a new entity. Run it in CI, and on a sample of live traffic by logging served values and recomputing them offline. Compare with explicit null handling, an agreed tolerance for floats computed by different engines, and over the union of keys so a missing row counts as a difference. When the check fails, the first differing column usually names the drift.

beats.recap: Import one transformation; if a port is unavoidable, test it on inputs that contain every edge case.

beats.title: A late reading adds a version; it never rewrites what was known
beats.outcome: Rerun with late-arriving data and state which training rows change and why the others must not.
beats.explanation: When PR-01's 09:50 reading arrives at 11:05, the 11:30 run publishes a second [[dbxfe-features-version-concept|feature version]] of the 10:00 window: 78.0 from three readings. Notice in the third state that only the 11:45 prediction changes; the 11:00 prediction keeps 77.0 because the late reading had not arrived. The fourth state shows the tempting shortcut: recomputing history once from all data stamps 10:30 on a row that used an 11:05 reading.

samajh.text: Bijli ka bill 5 tareekh ko us din tak ki meter reading se banta hai. Ek reading 12 tareekh ko der se aati hai, toh company ek naya, revised bill nikaalti hai; purana bill jaisa chhapa tha waisa hi rehta hai. Agar koi poochhe ki 6 tareekh ko aapke haath mein kaunsa bill tha, toh jawab purana bill hai, revised wala nahi.
samajh.mapping: Each bill is a feature version, its issue date is available_at and the question about the 6th is a prediction made between the two versions.
samajh.boundary: A revised bill replaces the amount owed; a new feature version never replaces history and serves only predictions made after its own publication.

handbook.markdown:
Append-only versions make time travel possible. The job keeps a signature per machine and window, here the reading count and the latest ingestion time, and publishes a new row only when it changes; nothing published is edited. After two late readings the table grows from six to eight rows:

| machine | window | published | temp | readings |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PR-01 | 10:00 | 10:30 | 77.0 | 2 |
| PR-01 | 10:00 | 11:30 | 78.0 | 3 |
| PR-02 | 08:00 | 08:30 | 65.5 | 2 |
| PR-02 | 08:00 | 12:30 | 66.0 | 3 |

The join then picks the newest window first and its newest version second, both among rows published by the prediction time. Exactly one training row changes, PR-01 at 11:45. PR-02's republished 08:00 window changes nothing, because its 10:00 window is newer; a plain `merge_asof` on `available_at` would wrongly pick that republished row for PR-02 at 12:45, which is why the lab tests for it.

Why not overwrite? An overwritten table answers only 'what do we know now'. Training needs 'what did we know then', and so do audits of past model decisions. The lineage column makes an overwrite detectable, because the contract refuses any row whose inputs arrived after its stated publication.

Late data also reaches labels: a corrected failure record is a label version with its own known-at time, and the serving module treats delayed labels in production monitoring. What to inspect after a rerun: rows added per window, proof that no published row changed, and the list of training rows whose values changed with their prediction and publication times. When a watermark guarantees no inputs arrive later than a stated delay, one publication after the watermark is simpler; write the watermark into the contract.

beats.recap: Late inputs append versions; each prediction keeps the version that existed at its time.

beats.title: One feature table can feed two models with two freshness limits
beats.outcome: Reuse a governed feature table for a second model and diagnose a cadence mismatch without changing the join.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-features-reuse-concept|Feature reuse]] shares the definition, the contract and the published rows; each consumer still owns its decision times and freshness limit. Notice in the second state that a handover model predicting at 10:00 and 12:00 always finds a window that is 120 minutes old, over its 90-minute limit, so no row is usable. The third state lists fixes that respect time; joining on the window end is not one of them.

handbook.markdown:
Reuse pays because the expensive parts, definitions, backfills, tests and governance, are paid once. Each consumer reads the table and never modifies it; in Lab L18 the second model builds its training set from the same six rows without recomputing anything, and a test proves the table is unchanged afterwards.

What is not shared is policy. Each consumer states its prediction times, its maximum feature age and its training cutoff. The failure model allows 180 minutes and finds eight usable rows. The handover model allows 90 minutes and predicts exactly when windows close, at 10:00 and 12:00. At those instants the newest published window ended two hours earlier, so every row is 120 minutes old and `stale`, and PR-03 at 10:00 has no row at all.

The join is correct; the cadence does not fit the decision. Options, cheapest first: move the decision after a publication (at 10:35 the 10:00 window is 35 minutes old); shift the window grid so a window closes and is published just before each handover (windows ending 09:30, published by 10:00); or compute the value on request from raw readings, which requires those readings at serving time. Publishing sooner alone cannot help a decision made at the instant a window closes. Loosening the limit to 180 minutes makes rows `ok` by accepting older information; that is the model owner's decision, not a data fix.

Before reusing a table, compare its cadence and publication delay with your decision times, its null meaning with your model's handling, and its contract version with the one you tested. Explaining it: 'The features are fine; they arrive on a schedule that does not match this decision.'

beats.recap: Share rows and definitions; own your decision times and freshness limit.

beats.title: Batch or online follows from when the decision is made
beats.outcome: Choose batch scoring, online lookup or on-demand computation for a decision from its timing, freshness and request-time inputs.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-features-delivery-concept|Batch versus online delivery]] is a requirement, not a taste. Notice in the first state that batch scoring reads the offline table on a schedule while online inference looks up a key when a request arrives, and each has its own silent failure. The second state places Cinderline's decisions: the 06:00 maintenance list is batch, a press-side alert is online, and the 10:00 handover score is neither until its owner moves it, because an online lookup then serves the same 120-minute-old row. The third separates precomputed windows from inputs known only in the request.

handbook.markdown:
Start from the decision, not the store. Four questions settle most cases: when is the decision made, on a schedule or when a request arrives; how old may inputs be at that moment; are any inputs known only in the request, such as an operator's die scan; and how many decisions per second at what latency.

Batch: a job joins features as of each scoring time, writes predictions with the model version and the feature timestamps used, and consumers read the stored results. Freshness equals the schedule, and the silent failure is a skipped or late run, so monitor the newest `available_at` used. Batch is cheaper, easier to reproduce and the default for lists, reports and planning.

Online: a service looks up each entity's newest published row at request time and scores it. Freshness equals the publication and sync cadence, and the silent failure is a stalled sync that keeps serving old rows, so return and log the feature timestamp with every response and apply the staleness rule the training set used.

On demand: a value that depends on the request itself is computed at request time by a function, and the same function must compute it for training rows from logged request inputs, or training and serving diverge.

Online does not repair a cadence mismatch. At 10:00 the newest published row for the handover model is the 08:00 window, so an online lookup serves the same 120-minute-old row the batch join finds; the fixes are the reuse beat's: the owner moves the decision to 10:35 and batch scores it, or the value is computed on demand from raw readings.

When not to go online: if the decision is made on a schedule, an online store adds a second copy of the data, a sync to monitor and another place for skew, for no gain. Explaining it to an operations lead: 'The morning list needs yesterday's data by 06:00; the press alert needs the last minutes' data within a second. They are different products.' The timings here are synthetic; real latency needs come from the process owner.

beats.recap: Scheduled decisions get batch features; request-time decisions get online or on-demand features.

beats.title: A time series feature table answers the as-of question only if its timestamp means usable
beats.outcome: Map the point-in-time join onto a Unity Catalog time series feature table and FeatureLookup and state what its timestamp key must mean.
beats.explanation: In Databricks Feature Store, a Unity Catalog table with a primary key is a feature table, and a TIMESERIES key makes it a [[dbxfe-features-timeseries-concept|time series feature table]]. A FeatureLookup with timestamp_lookup_key returns the latest value prior to each row's timestamp. Notice in the second state that if the timestamp key stores the window end, a 10:15 lookup returns the 10:00 window published at 10:30. The third stores publication time instead, and the lookup matches the lab's point-in-time join.

handbook.markdown:
The documented pieces and their conditions. Databricks Feature Store needs a workspace enabled for Unity Catalog. Any Delta table in Unity Catalog with a primary key can be a feature table. A time series feature table has one timestamp key of TimestampType or DateType, marked with the TIMESERIES keyword (Databricks Runtime 13.3 LTS and above), and no partition columns. An illustrative design, not executed here, stores the publication time as that key:

```sql
CREATE TABLE ml.press.sensor_features (
  machine_id STRING NOT NULL,
  available_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
  feature_time TIMESTAMP,
  temp_mean_2h DOUBLE,
  CONSTRAINT sensor_features_pk
    PRIMARY KEY (machine_id, available_at TIMESERIES))
```

```python
from datetime import timedelta
from databricks.feature_engineering import FeatureEngineeringClient, FeatureLookup

lookup = FeatureLookup(
    table_name="ml.press.sensor_features", lookup_key="machine_id",
    timestamp_lookup_key="prediction_time", lookback_window=timedelta(hours=3))
training_set = FeatureEngineeringClient().create_training_set(
    df=labels, feature_lookups=[lookup], label="label")
```

The glossary calls timestamp keys the event time associated with the feature value, and the lookup returns the latest values prior to each timestamp, or null. If the key holds the window end, a delayed publication leaks exactly as the event-time join did; storing the publication time makes 'prior to the prediction' mean 'published before it'. Test the equal-timestamp boundary yourself. With one timestamp key, a run that republishes an older window beside a newer one would create two rows for one key, and a republished older window would outrank the newer one. Publish at most one row per machine per run, holding that machine's newest window and version and only when it changes, and keep every version in a separate audit table.

`lookback_window` excludes values older than the timedelta (default None, any age) during training and batch inference, which matches the consumer's staleness limit. What the platform does not do for you: enforce uniqueness (keys are informational), store lineage, or check that your timestamp means availability. Verify runtime, client version and entitlement before relying on any of it.

beats.recap: Store when a value became usable as the timestamp key, and the platform's as-of lookup stays honest.

beats.title: Online lookup serves the newest published value, so the age rule moves to the caller
beats.outcome: Describe how feature tables reach online stores and serving endpoints, and what the lookback window does not do during online inference.
beats.explanation: An [[dbxfe-features-online-store-concept|online feature store]] keeps published rows ready for low-latency lookup, and Model Serving can look up a logged model's features automatically. Notice the second state: the documentation says the lookback window applies in training and batch inference, while online inference always uses the latest value. A row training would treat as stale is served. The third state closes the gap: return the feature timestamp, apply the same age rule and log what was served.

handbook.markdown:
Documented pieces, as reviewed for this module. Databricks Online Feature Stores are powered by Lakebase and sync data from offline Unity Catalog feature tables with three publish modes: TRIGGERED (the default, incremental on a schedule or by API), CONTINUOUS (streaming updates) and SNAPSHOT (a one-time full copy). Published tables need non-nullable primary keys, and Change Data Feed for TRIGGERED and CONTINUOUS. Model Serving with automatic feature lookup retrieves published values for models logged with `FeatureEngineeringClient.log_model`, so the most recent values are used. Feature Serving endpoints return feature values themselves to applications outside Databricks. On-demand features compute request-time values with Python user-defined functions, bound through `FeatureFunction` in training and evaluated automatically at inference.

The consistency gap to design for: the point-in-time documentation states that `lookback_window` is applied during training and batch inference, and that online inference always uses the latest value regardless of it. If PR-03's sensor stops, training marks its rows stale after three hours, while the online path keeps serving the last value indefinitely. Choose one remedy and apply it in both paths: include the feature's age as a feature, check age in the calling application and fall back, or have the producer publish an explicit no-data state.

Log what was served. For endpoints created from February 2025, Model Serving can log the augmented DataFrame with looked-up feature values to inference tables; comparing those rows with recomputed training rows is the live version of the lab's consistency check.

Caveats: online stores, Feature Serving and serverless options vary by cloud, region and entitlement, and names here have changed; the documentation keeps a migration page for legacy online tables. Check current pages, pricing and your workspace before promising latency, freshness or cost. Nothing here was deployed or measured.

beats.recap: Online inference serves the newest value; carry its age and enforce the training rule yourself.

beats.title: Point-in-time correctness is shown with tests that fail first
beats.outcome: Assemble evidence that a training set contains no future information and state what that evidence does not prove.
beats.explanation: A higher score is not evidence of a correct join; it is often evidence of a leak. Notice the first state: each deliberately wrong approach fails with a named reason, from the event-time join, two rows, to the overwrite backfill, refused by lineage. The second shows the real pipeline passing the same guards, with one training row changed by the late rerun. The third lists what these [[dbxfe-features-evidence-concept|leakage tests]] cannot show, including whether the features predict anything.

handbook.markdown:
Evidence has three layers. First, a guard over every training row: `available_at <= prediction_time` and `source_max_ingested_at <= prediction_time`, raising with the offending rows named. Second, tests that prove the guard bites: feed it an event-time join, a latest-value lookup, a duplicate key, a drifted port and a backfill, and assert each fails for its reason, not merely that something failed. Third, a rerun with late data showing which rows changed and that published rows did not.

Lab L18 packages this as 25 tests over hand-authored expected rows. Key outputs: the event-time join refused for PR-02 at 10:15 and PR-03 at 10:20; the latest-value lookup refused for seven rows; the drifted port refused on two windows at 10:30 and accepted at 08:30; one training row changed by the late readings; zero usable rows for the handover model at 90 minutes. These are local pandas executions on fictional data that demonstrate mechanism, not a platform and not a model.

An honest demonstration to a stakeholder shows one timeline with a delayed publication, the leaky join's row beside the corrected row, and the failing test that catches the leaky version. Say what changed in the numbers and why the corrected numbers may be lower. Do not present an accuracy improvement as proof of feature quality.

What the evidence does not show: that the features predict failures (no model was trained), behaviour at scale or under streaming, clock skew between systems, or how a particular platform version behaves. Those need their own evidence: evaluation on a forward period, load tests and verification in the target workspace. When reviewing someone else's evidence, ask whether the tests ever failed, whether the expected values were written independently of the code, and whether the fixture contains the edge cases the contract names.

beats.recap: Show the guard failing on known leaks, then passing on the real pipeline, and say what remains unproven.

extensionCards.prompt: What can go wrong if a feature table's primary key is declared with RELY while duplicates exist?
extensionCards.answer: Databricks may rewrite queries assuming the key is unique, and relying on an unsatisfied constraint can return incorrect results.
extensionCards.explanation: Primary key constraints on Databricks are informational and not enforced. The RELY option tells the optimizer it may exploit the constraint to rewrite queries; the documentation states that making sure the constraint holds is the user's responsibility, that relying on an unsatisfied constraint may lead to incorrect query results, and that these optimizations need Photon-enabled compute. A [[dbxfe-features-extension-rely-concept|RELY constraint]] on Cinderline's feature table is only safe while the pipeline's duplicate check keeps running before every publication: the constraint states a promise, it does not keep one.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It turns an unenforced key from a harmless label into a source of wrong answers once duplicates slip in.

extensionCards.prompt: Why can a missing-value indicator be absent for a column that is null only at serving time?
extensionCards.answer: SimpleImputer with add_indicator=True creates indicator columns only for features that had missing values during fit.
extensionCards.explanation: scikit-learn's SimpleImputer can stack a MissingIndicator onto its output with add_indicator=True, so a model can tell imputed values from measured ones. The documentation notes that a feature with no missing values at fit time does not appear in the indicator even if it has missing values at transform time. If Cinderline's training rows never had a null vib_max_2h but serving does, the served value is silently imputed with no flag. Make sure training data contains the missingness the contract allows, or configure a [[dbxfe-features-extension-indicator-concept|missing indicator]] for every feature, and test the serving path with a null.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It is a documented way for one pipeline object to treat serving-time nulls differently from training-time nulls.

extensionCards.prompt: How can Cinderline check the feature values that a served model actually received?
extensionCards.answer: Log the looked-up feature values with each request, recompute them offline for the same times and compare the two.
extensionCards.explanation: Model Serving with automatic feature lookup can log the augmented DataFrame, with looked-up feature values and function return values, to inference tables for endpoints created starting February 2025. Google's Rules of Machine Learning recommends monitoring training-serving skew explicitly, at least on a small fraction of traffic. Joining those [[dbxfe-features-extension-inference-log-concept|feature lookup logs]] to rows recomputed by the training transformation at the same request times turns the lab's 08:30 and 10:30 comparison into a production check that also catches stalled syncs. Confirm the logging configuration, retention and cost in your workspace first.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Offline tests cover fixtures; only logged serving inputs show what production actually fed the model.

extensionCards.prompt: What changes if Cinderline declares its two-hour windows as a Feature View instead of building a feature table?
extensionCards.answer: Databricks computes and materializes the declared features, including time-windowed aggregations, but Feature Views are in Public Preview.
extensionCards.explanation: The Databricks Feature Store page describes two authoring strategies: feature tables that you populate yourself, and Feature Views that define features declaratively while Databricks computes and manages the pipelines; Feature Views are recommended for most new cases, feature tables for flexible multi-stage batch work. Feature Views support sliding and tumbling time windows, and materialization creates Lakeflow pipelines that populate Unity Catalog tables for training, batch scoring or online serving. A [[dbxfe-features-extension-feature-views-concept|Feature View]] moves window and publication mechanics to the platform, so this module's questions become verification items: boundary rule, timestamp meaning, late-data handling and preview terms.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: It shows where the platform can own the mechanism and which of this module's checks still have to be verified.

recap.title: One row, two times, one rule
recap.markdown: **A feature row describes an entity over a window and becomes usable later; training must join on the second time.** A point-in-time join picks, among rows published by each prediction time, the newest window and then its newest version, or honestly nothing. Missing values get a rule per cause, identical in training and serving; zero is a measurement, not a blank. Keys are unique and checked, late data appends versions, and a lineage timestamp exposes backfills. One transformation serves both paths, and delivery follows when the decision is made. Databricks Feature Store provides time series lookups and online stores, but online inference ignores the lookback window, so age rules travel with the caller. **Transfer challenge:** an oil-analysis result is sampled at the press and entered six hours later; draw its timeline, pick its timestamp key and write the policy for a machine sampled nine hours ago.

appliedTask.title: Add a delayed lab feature without leaking it
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline adds oil_particles_ppm from oil samples: a sample is drawn at the press (sampled_at), analysed in a lab and entered about six hours later (result_entered_at); some results are corrected the next day. The failure model predicts every hour with a four-hour horizon. Design the feature row, the join, the missingness policy for machines without a usable result, how corrections are handled, the serving path, and the tests that would show the design leaks nothing.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: Feature row: machine_id, sampled_at (what the value describes), result_entered_at (when it became usable) and oil_particles_ppm, unique on all three keys, with a lineage check that the lab entry exists before the stated availability. Join: for each prediction, the newest sample among results entered at or before the prediction time, then its newest version; never join on sampled_at, which would leak six hours of lab time. Missingness: no result yet is none_available; a result older than a stated limit, for example 72 hours from sampling, is stale; both are excluded in training and get the same fallback in serving; never fill 0 ppm. Corrections append a version with the correction's entry time, so predictions before it keep the original. Serving: the hourly model can score in batch at five past each hour; if an online path is added, it serves the entry time with the value and applies the same age rule. Tests: a guard over every joined row, an event-time join on sampled_at failing by name, a duplicate sample refused, and a rerun with a correction showing only later predictions change.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer keeps the two times apart, chooses entry time as the join key, applies one missingness rule in both paths, treats corrections as versions and proves each property with a test that can fail. Choosing a different age limit is acceptable if the model owner states it.
